24.s: Whose production is counted in national income?
24.x: National income (NI) – The money value of all final goods and services produced by the normal residents of a country during a year – only final goods, so no double counting

24.s: What is national income the sum of, under the income view?
o: Factor incomes – wages, rent, interest, profit
24.x: Income view – NI = sum of factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) earned by normal residents – not government income, budget or PSU profits

24.s: Which kind of activity alone generates national income?
24.x: Source – Generated only from productive activity, not from any money-making activity

24.s: Which of these is a stock, not a flow, unlike national income?
24.x: Flow, not stock – NI is measured over a period; national wealth is a stock at a point of time

24.s: Why are national product and national income synonymous?
o: Output is distributed as factor incomes
24.x: Product = income – Output is distributed as factor incomes, so national product and national income are synonymous; production by labour and capital automatically generates income

24.s: Which of these is an economic activity?
o: A nurse paid in a charity hospital
24.x: Economic activity – Done for income or payment – e.g. a nurse paid in a charity hospital

24.s: What is an activity done for love or self-use, like teaching one's own child, called?
24.x: Non-economic activity – Done for love or self-use – tuition to one's own child, medicine for one's family, repairing one's own table

24.s: Which aggregate is national income defined as?
24.x: National income = NNP at factor cost – not GDP/GNP at market prices or NDP.

24.s: How is national income derived from NNP at market prices?
24.x: From NNP at MP – NI = NNP(MP) − (indirect taxes − subsidies)

24.s: How is national income derived from GNP at market prices?
24.x: From GNP at MP – NI = GNP(MP) − depreciation − indirect taxes + subsidies

24.s: How is national income derived from NDP at factor cost?
o: NDP(FC) + net factor income from abroad
24.x: From NDP – NI = NDP(FC) + net factor income from abroad

24.s: How is national product at factor cost derived from national product at market price?
24.x: National product at FC – National product at MP − indirect taxes + subsidies

24.s: What is done to move from market price to factor cost?
24.x: National product at FC – National product at MP − indirect taxes + subsidies

24.s: Which aggregate is NNP at factor cost equal to?
24.x: NNP at FC – = National Income

24.s: What is GDP(MP) if adding an NFIA of 10 gives a GNP of 120?
24.x: Example 1 – GDP(MP) 110 + NFIA 10 = GNP 120; − dep 15 = NNP(MP) 105; − NIT 5 = NI 100

24.s: What is GNP(MP) if GDP(MP) is 500 and NFIA is −10?
24.x: Example 2 – GDP(MP) 500, depreciation 50, NFIA −10, NIT 40 → GNP 490; NNP(MP) 440; NI 400

24.s: Why does national income count only final goods?
24.x: Only final goods – No double counting

24.s: Which is a non-economic activity?
o: A mother tutoring her own child
A doctor treating patients for fees
24.x: Non-economic activity – Tuition to one's own child, medicine for one's family, repairing one's own table (love or self-use)

24.s: What is national income if NNP(MP) is 440 and net indirect taxes are 40?
24.x: Worked example 2 – GDP(MP) 500, depreciation 50, NFIA −10, NIT 40 → GNP 490; NNP(MP) 440; NI 400

24.s: Which year's prices does real national income use?
24.x: Prices used – Current-year prices – Prices of a single base year

24.s: How does real national income treat the effect of price rise?
24.x: Includes price rise – Yes – No – price effect removed

24.s: What does nominal GDP (current prices) show?
o: Size of the economy in rupees
24.x: Use – Size of the economy in rupees – Growth of output

24.s: What does real GDP (constant prices) show?
24.x: Use – Size of the economy in rupees – Growth of output

24.s: What is the value of total production at the prices of a single base year called?
24.x: Real GDP – Value of total production at prices of a single year = GDP at constant prices

24.s: What is the market value of national output at base-year prices called?
24.x: Real national income – NI at constant prices; market value of national output in base-year prices = GNP at constant prices

24.s: How is real national income calculated?
o: Nominal NI divided by price index, times 100
24.x: Formula – Real NI = nominal NI ÷ price index × 100

24.s: What is real NI if nominal NI is Rs 20,000 crore and the price index is 250?
24.x: Example – Base 1990-91, NI Rs 20,000 crore, index 250 → Rs 8,000 crore

24.s: What happens to real income if prices and money income both double?
24.x: Prices and money income both doubled – Real income unchanged

24.s: At which prices does per capita income grow faster?
24.x: Per capita income – Grows faster at current prices – the constant-price series allows for the rise in the price level

24.s: How has India's GDP at market prices in rupees behaved over time?
24.x: India – GDP at market prices in rupees has risen steadily; real GDP growth has fluctuated (e.g. contraction in 2020-21)

24.s: What was India's nominal GDP growth in 2025-26 estimates (old series), with real growth at 7.4%?
24.x: Nominal vs real growth – Nominal exceeds real by roughly the inflation rate; 2025-26 estimates (old series): nominal 8.0%, real 7.4%

24.s: What was the base year of national accounts before the new series (2022-23)?

24.s: What was India's GDP at current prices in 2024-25 in the new series?
24.x: GDP at current prices 2024-25 – Rs 318.07 lakh crore (new series)

24.s: Which measure rises in a growing country?
24.x: Growth – Rise in real output: a growing country has rising GNP at constant prices; GDP growth data is the usual yardstick

24.s: What is the best sign of economic growth?
o: A sustained rise in real per capita income
24.x: Best measure / sign of growth – A sustained increase in real per capita income (per capita product)

24.s: Which of these is NOT a measure of economic growth?
o: Financial aid from the World Bank
24.x: Growth measures – GDP, GNP and per capita GNP – growth in financial aid from the World Bank is not one

24.s: What does 'c' denote in the consumption function C = C̄ + cY?
24.x: Consumption function – C = C̄ + cY – C = total consumption spending, C̄ = autonomous consumption, c = MPC

24.s: Which ratio is the slope of the consumption function?
24.x: MPC – ΔC/ΔY = slope of the consumption function

24.s: How is the marginal propensity to save (MPS) defined?
o: Total saving divided by total income
Change in consumption divided by change in income
Total consumption divided by total income
Change in saving divided by change in income
24.x: Saving – S = Y − C; MPS = ΔS/ΔY

24.s: What is the sum of MPC and MPS?
24.x: MPC and MPS – MPC + MPS = 1

24.s: What is autonomous spending?
24.x: Autonomous spending – Independent of income

24.s: What is consumption at zero income called?
24.x: Autonomous consumption (C̄) – Consumption even at zero income (from past savings or borrowing)

24.s: What is induced consumption?
24.x: Induced consumption – Changes with income

24.s: What is induced investment?
o: Investment that varies with national income
24.x: Induced spending / investment – Varies with the level of national income

24.s: What is the total demand for final goods and services in an economy called?
24.x: Aggregate demand – Total demand for final goods and services

24.s: What is an inventory in national income accounting?
24.x: Inventory – Stock of unsold goods

24.s: What is the multiplier if MPS is 0.25?
24.x: Multiplier (k) – k = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS – a low MPC gives a low multiplier; MPS 0.25 → k = 4

24.s: Who gave the accelerator concept (induced investment ÷ change in income)?
24.x: Accelerator – Induced investment ÷ change in income (J.M. Clark)

24.s: When is investment profitable in terms of the marginal efficiency of investment (MEI)?
o: When MEI is below the interest rate
When MEI exceeds the interest rate
24.x: Marginal efficiency of investment – Invest while MEI > interest rate: MEI 7% > 6% → profitable

24.s: What do 'ex-ante' values mean?
24.x: Ex-ante / ex-post – Planned (intended) values / actual (realised) values

24.s: Which of these affects the mobilisation of domestic savings?
24.x: Mobilisation of domestic savings – Depends on past behaviour, the propensity to save and tax policy

24.s: What is net investment if gross investment only covers depreciation?
24.x: Net investment – Gross − depreciation; gross investment that only covers depreciation → net investment zero

24.s: What does realised investment include besides planned investment?
24.x: Realised investment – Planned + unplanned (unintended change in inventories)

24.s: When is income in equilibrium in the Keynesian model?
24.x: Equilibrium – Planned saving = planned investment

24.s: After which war did pent-up consumer demand prevent an expected slump despite cuts in government purchases?
24.x: After World War II many economists expected a slump because of the sharp cut in government purchases at demobilisation; pent-up consumer demand prevented it.

24.s: How does an easy money policy shift the LM curve?
24.x: IS-LM: an easy money policy shifts the LM (L = M) curve right/down – interest falls, income rises; the IS (I = S) curve shifts right when autonomous spending rises at every interest rate (e.g. technology raising investment), and left with more saving, higher taxes or lower government purchases.

24.s: Which of these is added to national income to get personal income?
24.x: Personal income (PI) – NI − undistributed corporate profits − social security contributions − corporate tax + government and business transfer payments + net interest paid by government

24.s: How is personal disposable income derived from personal income?
o: PI − personal direct taxes − non-tax payments
24.x: Personal disposable income (PDI) – PI − personal direct taxes − non-tax payments (fines, fees); always less than PI

24.s: What is the difference between personal income and personal disposable income?
24.x: PI − PDI – = direct taxes

24.s: What is national income divided by to get per capita income?
24.x: Per capita income (PCI) – National income ÷ population = NNP ÷ total population (not GDP or NDP ÷ population)

24.s: How is NDP derived from GDP?
24.x: NDP – GDP − depreciation

24.s: How are national savings computed?
24.x: National savings – National disposable income − consumption

24.s: What does per capita income show about a country?
o: Standard of living and regional imbalances
24.x: Meaning – PCI = average income of a country; shows the standard of living and regional imbalances

24.s: Which is a better measure of welfare than GNP?
24.x: Welfare – PCI is a better welfare measure than GNP

24.s: When does per capita income fall even as national income rises?
o: When population grows faster than national income
24.x: PCI falls while NI rises – When population grows faster than NI; PCI rises only when NI grows faster than population

24.s: Why is India's GNP lower than its GDP?
24.x: GNP vs GDP – GNP is not always higher than GDP – India's NFIA is negative

24.s: Which aggregate is used to compare economies?
24.x: Comparing economies – GDP is used, not NDP

24.s: What is purchasing power?
o: The goods and services a person can buy
24.x: Purchasing power – The goods and services a person can buy – indicated by his income

24.s: Which is deducted from personal income to get personal disposable income?
o: Personal direct taxes and non-tax payments
24.x: Personal disposable income (PDI) – PI − personal direct taxes − non-tax payments (fines, fees); less than PI

24.s: Which aggregate divided by total population gives per capita income?
24.x: Per capita income (PCI) – National income ÷ population = NNP ÷ total population

24.s: What does national disposable income minus consumption give?
24.x: National savings – National disposable income − consumption

24.s: Which aggregate is per capita income a better welfare measure than?
24.x: PCI – PCI = average income of a country; shows the standard of living and regional imbalances; a better welfare measure than GNP

24.s: What must grow faster than population for per capita income to rise?
24.x: PCI falls while NI rises – When population grows faster than NI; PCI rises only when NI grows faster than population

24.s: What does GDP measure?
o: Final goods and services produced within the domestic territory
24.x: GDP (Gross Domestic Product) – Value of all final goods and services produced within the domestic territory of a country during a year, whoever produces them

24.s: Whose output does GNP measure?
o: Normal residents and their property, at home or abroad
24.x: GNP (Gross National Product) – Value of final goods and services produced by the normal residents and their property, inside or outside the country, in a year = Gross National Income

24.s: What is GDP based on?
24.x: Based on – Domestic territory (location) – Normal residents (nationality)

24.s: What is GNP based on?
24.x: Based on – Domestic territory (location) – Normal residents (nationality)

24.s: How are earnings of Indians abroad treated in India's GDP?
24.x: Indians earning abroad – Excluded – Included

24.s: How are earnings of Indians abroad treated in India's GNP?
24.x: Indians earning abroad – Excluded – Included

24.s: How is GNP linked to GDP?
24.x: Link – GDP = GNP − NFIA – GNP = GDP + NFIA

24.s: What is the main difference between GDP and GNP?
24.x: Main difference GDP vs GNP – Net factor income from abroad (not transfer payments or depreciation)

o: Factor income received from abroad − factor income paid abroad
24.x: NFIA – Factor income received from abroad − factor income paid to abroad

24.s: How is GNP derived from GDP?
o: GDP + net factor income from abroad

24.s: When can GDP equal GNP?
o: When NFIA is zero, e.g. a closed economy
24.x: GDP = GNP is possible – When NFIA = 0 (e.g. a closed economy)

24.s: What is India's NFIA usually like, making GNP lower than GDP?
24.x: India – NFIA usually negative → GNP below GDP

24.s: In which aggregate does income earned in Saudi Arabia by an Indian resident count?
24.x: Income earned in Saudi Arabia by an Indian resident – Counts in India's GNP only

24.s: What is the loss in value of fixed capital through wear and tear called?

24.s: How is NNP derived from GNP?
24.x: NNP – GNP − depreciation = GDP + NFIA − depreciation

24.s: What is the difference between GNP and NNP?
24.x: GNP − NNP – = depreciation

24.s: How is NNP at market prices derived?

24.s: How is GNP derived from NNP?

24.s: How is NDP at factor cost derived from GDP at market price?
o: GDP(MP) minus depreciation and net indirect taxes

24.s: What do PPP exchange rates compare?
o: Prices of the same basket of goods in different countries

24.x: India's PPP GDP vs market-rate GDP – Much larger, because prices are lower in India

24.s: How is market price related to factor cost?
o: FC plus indirect taxes minus subsidies
FC minus indirect taxes plus subsidies

o: GDP at MP − indirect taxes + subsidies

Income of the State's residents abroad

31.s: How many gig workers does NITI Aayog project for India by 2029-30?

32.s: What kind of economy is India, though it still shows underdeveloped features?

32.s: What is the main reason India is labelled a developing economy?

32.s: Which pair is listed among the salient features of the Indian economy?
o: High per capita income and full employment
Low per capita income and massive unemployment

32.s: What marks a developed economy, unlike India's predominance of agriculture?
32.x: Predominance of agriculture – The Indian economy is primarily an agricultural economy; industrial dominance marks a developed economy

32.x: Capital and labour – Low capital formation (needs a high savings rate) and low productivity of labour

32.s: What is the marginal productivity of surplus farm labour in a labour-surplus economy?

32.s: In which system are prices set by demand and supply rather than by the government?
32.x: Market system – Prices set by demand and supply, not by the government

32.s: What is an economy called in which neither exports nor imports take place?

32.s: Who is known as the Father of Economics?

32.s: In which year was Adam Smith's 'Wealth of Nations' published?
32.x: Adam Smith (Scottish) – Father of (Modern) Economics / of capitalism – *Wealth of Nations* (1776)

32.s: Which Keynesian idea says that if all save more, income falls and total saving may not rise?
32.x: J.M. Keynes – *General Theory*; modern macroeconomics; paradox of thrift – if all save more, income falls and total saving may not rise

32.s: Which book did Joan Robinson publish in 1956?
32.x: Joan Robinson – *The Accumulation of Capital* (1956)

32.s: Who: Dual-sector model: surplus labour from the subsistence to the modern sector?
32.x: W. Arthur Lewis – Dual-sector model: surplus labour from the subsistence to the modern sector

32.s: Who: Averages = "statistical constants which enable us to comprehend in a single effort the significance of the whole"?
32.x: A.L. Bowley – Averages = "statistical constants which enable us to comprehend in a single effort the significance of the whole"

32.s: Which word comes from the Greek 'oikonomia' (oikos = household, nomos = management)?
32.x: "Economics" comes from the Greek *oikonomia* (oikos = household, nomos = management).

32.s: Which of these is a fixed cost that does not vary with output?
32.x: Fixed cost – Does not vary with output – expenditure on machines (raw material, labour wages and traffic costs vary)

32.s: What are goods that are completely interchangeable called?
32.x: Perfect substitutes – Completely interchangeable goods; perfect complements are used together

32.s: Which effect must be stronger for the demand of a Giffen good to move with its price?
32.x: Giffen good – Inferior good; income and substitution effects oppose – demand can be inversely or positively related to price; if the income effect is stronger, demand moves with price

32.s: What is the marginal product when total product is at its maximum?
32.x: Total and marginal product – TP rising at an increasing rate → MP rises; at a diminishing rate → MP falls; TP maximum → MP zero; TP falling → MP negative

32.s: What is the law of increasing returns also called?
32.x: Increasing returns – Law of increasing returns = law of decreasing cost

32.s: What happens to total revenue when marginal revenue is zero?
32.x: Marginal revenue – MR > 0 → TR rises; MR = 0 → TR maximum; MR < 0 → TR falls

32.s: Besides the availability of close substitutes, what does the price elasticity of demand depend on?
32.x: Price elasticity of demand – Depends on the nature of the good and the availability of close substitutes

32.s: What are simplified representations of a theory, expressed in words, diagrams, tables or equations, called in economics?
32.x: Economic models – Simplify reality, represent a whole or part of a theory, show cause and effect; expressed in words, diagrams, tables or equations – not only equations

32.s: To which kind of models does the 'unit root' (Dickey-Fuller test) belong?
32.x: Unit root – A concept of time-series models (Dickey-Fuller test): a series with a unit root is non-stationary

32.s: When more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor, marginal product eventually falls. This is the law of?
32.x: Law of diminishing returns – More units of a variable factor added to a fixed factor → marginal product eventually diminishes

32.s: What must be raised in the same proportion to get constant returns to scale?
32.x: Constant returns to scale – Need all inputs raised in the same proportion; raising labour alone by 10% with capital fixed raises output by less than 10%

32.s: What is true of the elasticity of substitution between inputs in a CES production function?
32.x: CES production function – Elasticity of substitution between inputs is constant (Cobb-Douglas: the special case with elasticity 1)

32.s: How many inputs does an isoquant combine to show the same level of output?
32.x: Isoquant – All combinations of two inputs (labour and capital) that yield the same maximum possible level of output

32.s: What is the money actually paid to buy or hire factors of production called?
32.x: Explicit cost – Money actually paid to buy or hire factors of production

32.s: Which of these is an example of implicit (opportunity) cost?
o: Interest forgone on one's own funds
32.x: Implicit / opportunity cost – Return forgone on own resources – e.g. the interest he could earn by lending out his own funds

32.s: Which of these is a fixed cost on a farm?
32.x: Fixed cost (farm) – Does not vary with output – land rent, depreciation, interest on fixed capital (seeds, fertiliser, hired labour are variable)

32.s: Which cost curve is not U-shaped, falling continuously as a rectangular hyperbola?
32.x: AFC – Falls continuously (rectangular hyperbola) – the only cost curve that is not U-shaped (AVC, ATC, MC are U-shaped)

32.s: Why does long-run average cost (LAC) fall as output expands?
32.x: LAC – Falls as output expands because of economies of scale

32.s: How do factor prices and quantities move in an increasing-cost industry?
32.x: Increasing cost industry – Factor prices rise as the industry uses more factors (prices and quantities move in the same direction)

32.s: Which of these is NOT counted as cash in accounting?
32.x: Cash – Notes, coins, bank balances and cash equivalents; long-term investments are not cash

32.s: By which quantity is the marginal product of labour multiplied to get its value of marginal product (VMP)?
32.x: Value of marginal product (VMP) of labour – Marginal product of labour × price of output

32.s: What is total revenue minus total variable cost called in Marshall's terms?
32.x: Quasi-rent (Marshall) – Total revenue − total variable cost = fixed cost + profit → greater than the firm's total profit

32.s: Which of these is a feature of a perfect market?
o: Large number of buyers and sellers
32.x: Perfect market – Large number of buyers and sellers, homogeneous product, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge

32.s: What kind of demand curve do monopolistic competition and monopoly share?
32.x: Monopolistic competition and monopoly – Share a downward-sloping demand curve

32.x: Monopolistic competitor, long run – Never produces at the lowest point of LAC (tangency on the falling part → excess capacity)

32.s: Why can a pure monopolist keep pure profits in the long run?
32.x: Pure monopolist – Keeps pure profits in the long run because of blocked entry

32.s: When a competitive industry becomes a monopoly, what does the monopolist partly capture as profit?
32.x: Competitive industry → monopoly – Part of consumer surplus goes to the monopolist as economic profit (the rest is deadweight loss)

32.s: Who developed the theory of contestable markets?
32.x: Contestable markets (Baumol) – Even a few firms behave competitively if entry is absolutely free and exit entirely costless

32.s: What does each firm assume its rival keeps constant in the Cournot duopoly model?

32.s: Which duopoly model does not recognise interdependence yet gives a stable solution?
32.x: Cournot – Its quantity (output) constant – Interdependence not recognised; stable solution

32.s: What does each firm assume its rival keeps constant in the Bertrand duopoly model?
32.x: Bertrand – Its price constant – Price war down to competitive price

32.s: Which duopoly model ends in a price war down to the competitive price?
32.x: Bertrand – Its price constant – Price war down to competitive price

32.s: What does each firm assume its rival keeps constant in the Edgeworth duopoly model?
32.x: Edgeworth – Its price constant – Price oscillates – no stable solution

32.s: In which duopoly model does price oscillate with no stable solution?
32.x: Edgeworth – Its price constant – Price oscillates – no stable solution

32.s: What is a game called where one player's gain equals the other's loss?
32.x: Zero-sum game – One player's gain = the other's loss

32.s: Which strategy chooses the option that maximises the minimum gain?
32.x: Maximin – Choose the strategy that maximises the minimum gain (minimax = minimise the maximum loss)

32.s: Besides the production function, to what does Pareto's welfare analysis relate?
32.x: Pareto's welfare analysis – Relates to the production function and utility (no one can be made better off without making someone worse off)

32.s: Which condition defines general equilibrium of production and exchange (2 persons, 2 goods)?

MRS of A > MRS of B

32.x: Consumption (exchange) contract curve – Locus of general-equilibrium points of exchange

32.x: Grand utility-possibility curve – Locus of Pareto optimality in both production and consumption

32.x: Social welfare function – Needs an ethical (value) judgement – Pareto optimality alone cannot rank its points

32.s: Besides technical efficiency, what does productive efficiency combine?
32.x: Productive efficiency – Factor-price (allocative) efficiency + technical efficiency

32.s: For what are shadow (accounting) prices used in public-sector project appraisal?

32.x: Shadow (accounting) prices – Imputed values of costs and benefits, used in public-sector project appraisal as a sound basis for allocation decisions

32.s: What does a shadow price measure in linear programming?

32.x: Shadow price in linear programming – Change in the objective function per unit change in a constraint

32.s: Which returns to scale does linear programming assume?
32.x: LP assumptions – Linearity, i.e. constant returns (increasing returns to scale is not assumed)

69.x: CPI (Rural / Urban / Combined) – NSO, MoSPI (earlier CSO) – 2024 (replaced 2012; first release 12 Feb 2026 for Jan 2026) – Headline inflation; RBI's inflation target

69.x: CPI-IW (Industrial Workers) – Labour Bureau, Ministry of Labour and Employment – 2016 (from Sep 2020) – Dearness allowance of industrial workers and Central Government employees

69.x: CPI-UNME (Urban Non-Manual Employees) – CSO – the only one of the four labour/worker CPIs not compiled by the Labour Bureau – 1984-85 – Discontinued from January 2011 after CPI-Urban began

69.s: For what is the WPI mainly used?
69.x: WPI – Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry – 2022-23 (revised 2026; earlier 2011-12, 2004-05) – Wholesale prices; contract escalation

69.x: CFPI (Consumer Food Price Index) – NSO – Same as CPI – Food inflation

69.x: GDP deflator – NSO – National-accounts base – Widest measure – all goods and services produced

69.s: Which is the widest measure of inflation, covering all goods and services produced?
69.x: GDP deflator – NSO – National-accounts base – Widest measure – all goods and services produced

69.x: CPI-IW base – 1982 → 2001 → 2016 (w.e.f. September 2020)

69.x: Labour Bureau – Set up 1920, at Chandigarh, under the Ministry of Labour and Employment

69.s: On which index is dearness allowance fixed?
69.x: Dearness allowance (DA) – Fixed on the Consumer Price Index – CPI-IW; linking pay to a price index is indexation ("fixing of wage compensation")

69.s: Who prepares India's national income and GDP estimates?

69.s: What does a retail price index track?
o: Average cost of living of households
69.x: Retail price index – Change in the average cost of living of households (a basket of retail prices)

69.s: Up to which month was WPI India's headline inflation measure?
69.x: WPI was India's headline / "primary" / most common inflation measure till April 2014.

69.s: When did the RBI adopt CPI (Combined) as its key inflation measure?
69.x: April 2014: RBI adopted CPI (Combined) as its key measure (Urjit Patel Committee); headline inflation is now based on CPI-C, while CPI, WPI and the labour CPIs are all still published.

69.s: How is India's inflation rate usually calculated?
69.x: Inflation rate = year-on-year % change in CPI (current month's CPI over the CPI of the same month last year).

69.s: Which of these is NOT covered by the Wholesale Price Index?
69.x: Coverage – Prices of goods traded in bulk (first point); no services – CPI covers goods and services

69.s: How many items did the 2011-12 WPI series cover?

69.s: How many items does the new WPI (base 2022-23) cover?

69.s: What does the Producer Price Index measure?
69.x: PPI – Average change in prices received by producers (output PPI: goods leaving production; input PPI: inputs entering it)

69.s: How often were WPI figures for primary articles and fuel released until 2012?
69.x: Release – Weekly (primary articles, fuel) until 2012, so in 2010 it was not only monthly

69.s: Which price index gives less weight to food than CPI-IW?
69.x: Food weight – WPI gives less weight to food than CPI-IW

69.s: When was the WPI with base 2004-05 introduced?
69.x: Base 2004-05 series – Introduced on 14 September 2010

69.s: How many items does the new CPI (base 2024) cover?
69.x: New CPI (base 2024): 12 divisions (COICOP 2018), 358 items; food and beverages 36.75% (about 46% in the 2012 series); 12 online platforms and rural house rent added. Food has a bigger weight in CPI than in WPI.

69.s: Which committee revised the WPI to base 2004-05?
69.x: Abhijit Sen (2007; report May 2008) – WPI revision – base 2004-05

69.s: Which committee revised the WPI to base 2011-12?
69.x: Saumitra Chaudhuri (2012) – WPI revision – base 2011-12

69.s: Who headed the NITI Aayog group (2025) on the WPI with base 2022-23?
69.x: Ramesh Chand (NITI Aayog, 2025) – WPI base 2022-23

69.s: Which committee recommended CPI as the nominal anchor for monetary policy?
69.x: Urjit Patel (2014) – CPI as nominal anchor; flexible inflation targeting

69.s: How is the GDP deflator calculated?
69.x: GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100 – the broadest measure (all goods and services produced).

69.s: What does a rise in the GDP deflator mean for the purchasing power of money?
69.x: A rise in the GDP/GNP deflator = rising prices → fall in the purchasing power of money.

69.s: Which inflation is "too much money chasing too few goods"?
69.x: Demand-pull – Aggregate demand > aggregate supply: expansionary fiscal and monetary policy, fiscal stimulus, higher purchasing power, rising money supply – "too much money chasing too few goods"

69.s: Which inflation comes from a rise in wages, raw-material and fuel prices?
69.x: Cost-push – Rise in prices of factors of production (wages, raw materials, fuel) → supply falls while demand is constant

69.s: Which inflation arises from poor farm productivity and supply bottlenecks?
69.x: Structural / bottleneck – Deficiencies in the economy – poor farm productivity, supply bottlenecks, inefficient distribution and storage; persists long and is hard for government to tackle

69.s: What kind of inflation arises when strong foreign demand drains domestic supply?
69.x: Export-led – Strong export demand drains domestic supply

69.s: What is the excess of aggregate demand over aggregate supply at full-employment output called?
69.x: Inflationary gap – Excess of aggregate demand (spending) over aggregate supply at full-employment output

69.s: Which of these is NOT a demand-pull cause?
69.x: Not demand-pull causes – Inflation-indexing of wages (cost side) and rising interest rates (they cut demand)

69.s: Which inflationary pressure does a permanent fall in input costs reduce?
69.x: Input costs – A permanent fall in input costs reduces cost-push pressure

69.s: Through which mechanism do inflation expectations feed inflation?
69.x: Inflation expectations – Also feed inflation (wage-price spiral)

69.s: What does a leftward shift of the supply curve mean?
o: More is supplied at the same price
The same quantity is supplied only at a higher price
69.x: Decrease in supply – Supply curve shifts left – the same quantity is supplied only at a higher price; extension/contraction are movements along the curve

69.s: Which of these is a demand-side cause of price rise in India?
69.x: Demand – Increase in money supply, rise in non-developmental public expenditure, deficit financing / deficit budget, loose monetary policy, rapid GDP growth, population growth

69.s: Which of these is a supply-side cause of price rise in India?
69.x: Supply – Erratic / less agricultural production, hoarding, higher MSPs, rise in crude oil and fertiliser prices (oil shocks), inefficient storage and marketing, rupee depreciation, cartelisation

69.s: Which of these can cause a general price rise?
69.x: General price rise may come from more money supply, lower aggregate output and higher effective demand.

69.s: Which demand factor drives food inflation in India?
69.x: Food inflation: changing consumption pattern with rising incomes and structural constraints in the food supply chain.

69.s: What is the dominant cause of inflation in India?
69.x: Supply shocks (erratic monsoon, El Nino, costlier crude, rupee depreciation) are the dominant cause of inflation in India; better storage and distribution efficiency eases them.

69.s: Which of these works against inflation management?
69.x: An unstable currency works against inflation management; stability, sound monetary policy and balanced supply-demand help.

69.s: Which North Sea crude grade is used as an oil price benchmark?
69.x: Brent (North Sea), West Texas Intermediate (WTI) (US) and Dubai – grades of crude oil used as price benchmarks; oil-price shocks feed cost-push inflation.

69.s: What is the essential attribute of inflation?
69.x: Inflation – A sustained rise in the general price level and a fall in the purchasing power (value) of money; the essential attribute is increase in prices

69.s: What happens to the purchasing power of money when all prices rise?
69.x: During inflation – Prices increase; when all prices rise, the purchasing power of money decreases

69.s: What does a rise in a commodity's price mean in money terms?
o: A rise in the value of currency
A fall in the value of currency
69.x: Rise in a commodity's price – Fall in the value of currency and rise in the value of the commodity (in money terms)

69.s: What is economic growth usually coupled with?
69.x: Economic growth – Usually coupled with (moderate) inflation – rising income and demand push prices up

69.s: What is a persistent fall in the general price level called?
69.x: Deflation – Persistent fall in the general price level (negative inflation) – not a currency fall or a fall in the inflation rate

69.s: What is a fall in the rate of inflation, which stays positive, called?
69.x: Disinflation – Fall in the rate of inflation, still positive (e.g. 3% → 2%)

69.s: What is inflation returning after deflation, a sign of recovery, called?
69.x: Reflation – Inflation returning after deflation – sign of recovery

69.s: What is high inflation with stagnant output and high unemployment called?
69.x: Stagflation – High inflation + slow growth / stagnant output + high unemployment

69.s: What is inflation in some items like food while others are stable called?
69.x: Skewflation – Inflation in some items (e.g. food) while others are stable or falling

69.s: What does a fall in the inflation rate mean?
69.x: A fall in the inflation rate means only that prices are rising more slowly.

69.s: What, combined with declining industrial production and sluggish growth, gives stagflation?
69.x: Inflationary pressure (e.g. from higher government spending) plus declining industrial production and sluggish growth → stagflation.

69.s: Which of these pulls prices down rather than creating inflation?
69.x: A fall in aggregate demand and currency appreciation pull prices down – they slow growth but do not create the inflation half of stagflation.

69.s: What is gradual inflation below about 3% called?
69.x: Creeping – Gradual, below about 3%

69.s: What rate of inflation is called walking or trotting inflation?
69.x: Walking / trotting – 3-10%

69.s: What is inflation at double or triple digits a year called?
69.x: Galloping – Double or triple digit (20%, 100%, 200% a year)

69.s: What is large, accelerating inflation where prices shoot up overnight called?
69.x: Hyperinflation – Large and accelerating; prices shoot up overnight

69.s: What does the RBI do with government securities to cut money in circulation?
69.x: Monetary (RBI) – Decrease money circulation: raise repo, reverse repo, Bank Rate, CRR, SLR; sell government securities (OMO) – reducing interest rates works the other way

69.s: Which type: Cut non-developmental spending, avoid deficit financing, raise direct taxes, cut indirect taxes on essentials?
69.x: Fiscal (Government) – Cut non-developmental spending, avoid deficit financing, raise direct taxes, cut indirect taxes on essentials

69.s: Which of these is a supply or administrative measure against inflation?
69.x: Supply / administrative – Control demand, rationing, prevent hoarding and black marketing, ban exports of scarce goods, suspend futures trading, buffer stocks

69.s: Which approach does controlling supply-side inflation need?
o: A mix of monetary, fiscal and exchange-rate policies
69.x: Control needs a combination of monetary, fiscal and exchange-rate policies – monetary policy alone cannot fix supply-side inflation; the RBI has the key role alongside the Government.

69.s: In which year was levy sugar under the dual price policy abolished?
69.x: Dual price policy – Sugar – a share of output (levy sugar) bought at a controlled price for the PDS, the rest sold in the open market (levy abolished 2013)

69.s: With which commodities did the Price Stabilisation Fund (2014-15) begin?
69.x: Price Stabilisation Fund (PSF) – Central Sector Scheme, 2014-15 (launched March 2015); began with onion and potato; pulses added later

69.s: Which subsidised product helped contain wheat inflation?
69.x: Bharat Atta – Subsidised wheat flour – helped contain wheat inflation

69.s: At what price was Bharat Chana Dal sold from July 2023?
69.x: Bharat Dal – Chana dal (July 2023), extended to moong dal; sold via NAFED, NCCF, Kendriya Bhandar; Bharat Chana Dal at ₹60/kg from July 2023

69.s: Who sells wheat and rice under the Open Market Sale Scheme (Domestic)?
69.x: OMSS (Domestic) – FCI sells wheat and rice

69.s: To what was the onion export duty cut on 13 Sep 2024?
69.x: Onion exports – Ban lifted 4 May 2024 with 40% duty and US$550 MEP; MEP removed and duty cut to 20% on 13 Sep 2024; NCCF and NAFED released 47,786 MT of PSF onion (to 8 Oct 2025)

69.s: What is described as the RBI's biggest concern?
69.x: RBI's biggest concern – Inflation

69.s: What was the repo rate after 7 Oct 2026?
69.x: Repo rate (7 Oct 2026) – 5.50% (5.25% in Aug 2026); repo acts on demand and cannot directly fix supply shocks (onion, crude oil)

69.s: What are principal and/or interest linked to in Inflation-Indexed Bonds?
69.x: Design – Principal and/or interest linked to an inflation index → protect investors from uncertainty about inflation (real return)

69.s: How do Inflation-Indexed Bonds help the government?
69.x: For government – Can reduce coupon rates on its borrowing (no inflation-risk premium)

69.s: How are interest and capital gains on Inflation-Indexed Bonds treated for tax?
69.x: Tax – Interest and capital gains are taxable

69.s: Who issued Inflation-Indexed Bonds in 2013?
69.x: Issued – By the RBI in 2013

69.s: Who heads the State-level Price Monitoring Committee?
69.x: State-level Price Monitoring Committee headed by the Chief Secretary; DES monitors 8 essential commodities daily (groundnut and palm oil added Feb 2025).

69.s: How many essential commodities does the DES monitor daily (after groundnut and palm oil were added)?
69.x: State-level Price Monitoring Committee headed by the Chief Secretary; DES monitors 8 essential commodities daily (groundnut and palm oil added Feb 2025).

69.s: Who loses from inflation?
69.x: Holders of real assets, equity investors – Bond / debenture holders, savings-account holders

69.s: Who benefits from inflation?
69.x: Rule: inflation benefits debtors, not bond-holders, consumers or fixed-income groups. With a price hike, businessmen generally gain (though not all) and consumers must curtail needs.

69.s: What are the costs of re-pricing goods during inflation called?
69.x: Other effects: falling saving (MPS falls), shift to gold, rising inequality, wage-price spiral, fewer exports; food inflation is regressive (the poor spend more of income on food); menu costs of re-pricing.

69.s: Who gains when the purchasing power of money rises in deflation?
69.x: Purchasing power of money rises → fixed-income groups (pensioners, salary earners) and creditors gain; debtors lose (heavier real debt).

69.s: What is the chain of postponed purchases, lower profits and higher unemployment called?
69.x: Deflationary spiral: postponed purchases → lower profits → higher unemployment → heavier real debt burden.

69.s: Which inflation measure includes food and energy prices?
69.x: Covers – Total inflation, including food and energy (oil, gas) – Excludes volatile food and fuel / energy

69.s: Which inflation shows the raw figure that consumers feel?
69.x: Shows – Raw figure – what consumers feel – Underlying, long-run trend

69.s: What does core inflation show?
69.x: Shows – Raw figure – what consumers feel – Underlying, long-run trend

69.s: Which is more volatile, headline or core inflation?
69.x: Volatility – More volatile – More stable

69.s: What does core inflation exclude from the CPI?
69.x: Index – Change in CPI-Combined (basket of a typical family) – CPI excluding food and fuel

69.s: What is inflation measured leaving out commodities with volatile prices called?
69.x: Inflation that leaves out commodities with volatile prices = core inflation.

69.s: Which index measures food inflation?
69.x: Food inflation: measured by the CFPI (10 sub-groups; cereals carry the highest weight).

69.s: What is a price index?
o: A statistical device to measure price changes
69.x: Price index – A statistical device to measure changes in the general price level

69.s: Which price index uses base-year quantities as weights?
69.x: Laspeyres index – Base-year (initial-year) quantities as weights

69.s: Which price index uses current-year quantities as weights?
69.x: Paasche index – Current-year weights

69.s: Which price index is the geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices?
69.x: Fisher's ideal index – Geometric mean of the two

69.s: Which economist is most associated with index numbers and the "ideal index"?
69.x: Irving Fisher – Economist most associated with index numbers (ideal index, tests of index numbers)

69.s: Which phase of the business cycle follows the peak or boom?
69.x: Business cycle phases: expansion / recovery (real GDP rising) → peak / boom → recession (falling) → trough / depression (bottom).

69.s: In which period: CPI-Combined 3.41% (3-year low, after demonetisation)?
69.x: December 2016 – CPI-Combined 3.41% (3-year low, after demonetisation)

69.s: What CPI inflation did the RBI project for 2024-25 at its Feb 2024 MPC?
How did food, headline and core inflation rank in early 2024?
69.x: Early 2024 – Food > Headline > Core; retail inflation eased (5.7% Dec 2023 → about 5.1% Jan 2024)

69.s: What was India's CPI inflation in 2025, a 12-year low?
69.x: 2025 (year) – CPI 2.2% (12-year low); food -0.2% → Core > Headline > Food; Oct 2025 0.3%

69.s: What was AP's retail inflation in May 2026, against India's 3.9%?
69.x: May 2026 – Headline 3.93%, food 4.85%, core 3.73% → Food > Headline > Core; AP 4.9% vs India 3.9%

69.s: What was CPI inflation in June 2026, the first breach of 4% in the new series?
69.x: June – Aug 2026 – 4.38% (June, first breach of 4% in the new series) → 4.8% (Aug, 20-month high); WPI (2022-23 base) 9.87% in June – West Asia fuel costs

69.s: In which year did the Urjit Patel Committee recommend CPI as the nominal anchor?
69.x: Urjit Patel Committee – 2014 – CPI as nominal anchor

69.s: When was the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement signed?
69.x: Monetary Policy Framework Agreement – Feb 2015 – Led to RBI Act amendment

69.s: What did the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement of 2015 lead to?
69.x: Monetary Policy Framework Agreement – Feb 2015 – Led to RBI Act amendment

69.s: In which year was the RBI Act amended to make flexible inflation targeting statutory?
69.x: RBI Act 1934 amended – 2016 – Statutory flexible inflation targeting; Sec 45ZA target set by Centre with RBI every 5 years; Sec 45ZB six-member MPC; Sec 45ZN report after 3 consecutive quarters of breach (first invoked 2022)

69.s: What is the upper tolerance limit of India's inflation target for 2026-31?
69.x: Target (1 Apr 2026 – 31 Mar 2031) – 4% CPI-Combined ± 2% (2-6%); 6% is only the upper limit

69.s: To what level did average CPI inflation fall under the inflation-targeting framework, from 6.8% in 2012-16?
69.x: Result – Average CPI fell from 6.8% (2012-16) to about 4.9% under the framework

69.s: What is the shape of the long-run Phillips curve according to Friedman?
69.x: Phillips curve (A.W. Phillips, 1958) – Inverse relation between unemployment and (wage) inflation; Friedman: long-run curve vertical; India's curve is flat (about 92% informal workers)

70.s: What is the largest item of Union revenue expenditure?
70.x: Largest item of Union revenue expenditure – Interest payments – larger than defence, subsidies, pensions or grants to States; also the largest non-plan item (1991-92 onwards)

70.s: How much is budgeted for interest payments in BE 2026-27?

70.s: What share of total Union spending was revenue expenditure in 2014-15?

70.s: What share of GDP was Centre plus States spending, per the Economic Survey 2016-17?
70.x: Centre + States spending – ≈ 28% of GDP (Economic Survey 2016-17)

70.s: What is total Union spending in BE 2026-27?

70.s: Which of these is a reason public spending grows?

70.x: States' share of taxes – 18% – 22%

70.s: What share of each rupee spent goes to States' share of taxes in BE 2026-27?

70.x: Defence – 8% – 11%

70.s: What share of each rupee spent goes to defence in BE 2026-27?

70.s: What share of each rupee spent goes to major subsidies in BE 2026-27?

70.s: What makes an expenditure capital rather than revenue?
70.x: Test – Changes the government's assets or liabilities = capital; the rest = revenue; capital expenditure buys, creates, upgrades or extends the life of assets

70.s: Which deficit is revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts?
70.x: Revenue deficit – Revenue expenditure − revenue receipts

70.s: What does the "Golden Rule" of public finance say?
70.x: Golden Rule – Borrow only for asset creation (capital expenditure)

70.s: What kind of expenditure is acquiring new technology for a firm?
70.x: Firms – Acquiring new technology = capital expenditure; debt vs equity is a way of financing, not a type of expenditure

70.s: Which parts did plan expenditure have?
70.x: Plan expenditure – Had both revenue and capital parts

70.s: What estimation method fixes a minimum amount per head?
70.x: Per capita method – Estimation that fixes a minimum amount per head

70.s: What is keeping spending within the sanctioned budget and laid-down rules called?
70.x: Budget control – Keeps spending within the sanctioned budget and the laid-down rules

70.s: With which Budget did the plan/non-plan split end?
70.x: End of the split – Plan/non-plan split ended with Budget 2017-18 (end of 12th Plan), announced in the Budget Speech 2016-17; replaced by revenue vs capital

70.s: From which year's budget did AP also drop the plan/non-plan split?
70.x: Andhra Pradesh – Also dropped it from its 2017-18 Budget

70.s: Who chaired the 2011 committee that called the plan/non-plan split "dysfunctional"?
70.x: C. Rangarajan High Level Expert Committee on Efficient Management of Public Expenditure (Planning Commission, 2011) – The split was "dysfunctional", an obstacle to outcome-based budgeting → remove it

70.s: Which was the largest non-plan item?
70.x: Non-plan items – Interest payments (largest), defence, subsidies (food, fertiliser), salaries, pensions, loans to States/UTs/PSUs

70.s: What kind of spending was plan expenditure regarded as?
70.x: Nature – Plan = asset-creating, productive; non-plan = consumptive, committed

70.s: To which side was maintenance of completed Plan assets shifted?

72.x: Distribution – Reduce inequality: progressive taxation + progressive expenditure

72.s: Which Musgrave function of fiscal policy aims to control inflation and unemployment?
72.x: Stabilisation – Control inflation and unemployment – minimising the risk of inflation is a fiscal aim

72.s: Which of these is a fiscal policy objective?
72.x: Fiscal objectives – Economic growth, distributive justice and price stability, full employment, resource mobilisation, balanced regional development

72.s: Which of these is NOT a fiscal policy objective?
72.x: Outside fiscal objectives – Regulation of inter-state trade; directing interest rates and managing money supply are monetary objectives

72.s: Which of these is an objective of monetary policy?
72.x: Monetary policy objectives – Economic growth, full employment, exchange stabilisation and price stability – exchange-rate stability is the monetary marker

72.s: What share of total taxes were direct taxes in FY25?
72.x: Progressive taxation – Tax rate rises as income rises, so the rich pay a larger share – reduces income inequality; direct taxes = 58.8% of total taxes (FY25)

72.s: Which of these is a fiscal policy tool?
72.x: Fiscal tools – Taxation (tax policy), public expenditure (capex as pump priming), public borrowing/debt, the budget, subsidies/DBT, transfer payments, deficit financing

72.s: Which of these is a monetary policy tool?
72.x: Monetary tools – Interest rate, CRR, bank rate, credit ceiling

72.s: What risk does external public borrowing carry?
72.x: Public borrowing – Internal and external; external borrowing carries currency risk

72.s: What share of GDP is Centre plus States spending, per ES 2016-17?
72.x: Public expenditure – Centre + States ≈ 28% of GDP (ES 2016-17); Union alone 13.6% (BE 2026-27)

72.s: Who makes fiscal policy in India?
72.x: Fiscal – Govt (MoF) – Taxation, expenditure, public debt, subsidies – Slow (budget cycle)

72.s: Which of these is a fiscal tool?
72.x: Fiscal – Govt (MoF) – Taxation, expenditure, public debt, subsidies – Slow (budget cycle)

72.s: How fast does fiscal policy act compared with monetary policy?
72.x: Fiscal – Govt (MoF) – Taxation, expenditure, public debt, subsidies – Slow (budget cycle)

72.s: Who makes monetary policy in India?
72.x: Monetary – RBI / MPC – Repo, CRR, SLR, OMOs, LAF – Fast (MPC bi-monthly)

72.s: Which of these is a monetary tool?
72.x: Monetary – RBI / MPC – Repo, CRR, SLR, OMOs, LAF – Fast (MPC bi-monthly)

72.s: How often does the MPC meet, making monetary policy fast?
72.x: Monetary – RBI / MPC – Repo, CRR, SLR, OMOs, LAF – Fast (MPC bi-monthly)

72.s: How is monetary policy related to fiscal policy?
72.x: Monetary policy is complementary to fiscal policy.

72.s: Which policy is ineffective in the classical range of IS-LM?
72.x: IS-LM classical range (vertical LM): fiscal policy is ineffective (full crowding out) even if investment is interest-elastic; monetary policy is effective.

72.s: What is government policy on taxation, expenditure and public debt called?
72.x: Fiscal policy – Government policy on taxation, expenditure and public debt (its income, spending and debt) to shape aggregate demand, allocation and distribution

72.s: From which Latin word, meaning basket or public purse, does "fiscal" come?
72.x: Word – From Latin fiscus = basket / public purse

72.s: Which division prepares the Union Budget?
72.x: Formulated by – The Ministry of Finance; Union Budget prepared by the Budget Division, Department of Economic Affairs (DEA)

72.s: What does Article 112 call the Budget?
72.x: Article 112 – Calls the Budget the "Annual Financial Statement"; the word "Budget" is not in the Constitution

72.s: Of which policy is the Union Budget an instrument?
72.x: Budget – An instrument of fiscal policy

72.s: Which crisis did Keynes present fiscal policy as the main tool against?
72.x: J.M. Keynes – *General Theory* (1936); fiscal policy as the tool against the Great Depression

72.s: Which Finance Minister laid the Long-Term Fiscal Policy in Parliament in Dec 1985?
72.x: V.P. Singh – Long-Term Fiscal Policy, laid in Parliament Dec 1985 (Budget year 1985-86) as Finance Minister

72.s: Which tax reform did the Long-Term Fiscal Policy introduce in the 1986-87 Budget?
72.x: LTFP's key reform – MODVAT – introduced in the 1986-87 Budget (from 1 March 1986), on L.K. Jha Committee lines

72.s: Who popularised the term "fiscal federalism" in 1959?
72.x: Richard Musgrave – Three budget functions; differential tax incidence; popularised "fiscal federalism" (1959)

72.s: Who chaired the RBI Advisory Group on Fiscal Transparency (2001)?
72.x: Montek Singh Ahluwalia – Chaired the RBI Advisory Group on Fiscal Transparency (report 2001)

72.s: In which year was the N.K. Singh FRBM Review Committee set up?
72.x: N.K. Singh – Committee 2016, report 2017: general govt debt 60% = Centre 40% + States 20%

72.s: Why is the fiscal deficit always larger than the primary deficit?
72.x: FD and PD – FD > PD always (interest is positive); PD = FD − interest

72.s: Why is the fiscal deficit usually larger than the revenue deficit?
o: It also covers borrowing for capital spending
72.x: FD and RD – FD > RD in practice (FD also covers borrowing for capital spending)

72.s: How does the effective revenue deficit compare with the revenue deficit?
72.x: ERD and RD – ERD ≤ RD

72.s: How does the fiscal deficit compare with the budgetary deficit?
72.x: FD and budgetary deficit – FD > budgetary deficit: FD also counts borrowings (incl. from the RBI) and other liabilities

72.s: Which is the largest deficit in the Union budget?
72.x: Largest deficit in the GoI budget – Fiscal deficit; descending order fiscal > revenue > primary (2026-27 BE: 4.3 > 1.5 > 0.7)

72.s: What does a zero primary deficit mean?
72.x: Zero primary deficit – FD = interest; borrowing just equals interest payment – debt-trap signal

72.s: What is borrowing to make interest payments called?
72.x: Debt trap – Borrowing to make interest payments

72.s: What does a zero revenue deficit mean?
72.x: Zero RD – Balanced revenue budget

72.s: What does a primary surplus mean?
o: Non-interest spending is covered by non-debt receipts
72.x: Primary surplus – Non-interest spending covered by non-debt receipts

72.s: What does an expansionary fiscal stance involve?
72.x: Expansionary – More spending / lower taxes – Recession; inflation risk

72.s: What does a contractionary fiscal stance involve?
72.x: Contractionary – Less spending / higher taxes – Overheating

72.s: When is a contractionary fiscal stance used?
72.x: Contractionary – Less spending / higher taxes – Overheating

72.s: What effect does a neutral fiscal stance have?
72.x: Neutral – Balanced effect – Stable times

72.s: When is a neutral fiscal stance used?
72.x: Neutral – Balanced effect – Stable times

72.s: What should the government do to fight a recession?
72.x: Recession – Increase expenditure on public projects; fiscal stimulus = cutting tax rates + more government spending (abolishing subsidies is not stimulus)

72.s: What is a counter-cyclical fiscal policy?
o: Deficits in slumps, consolidation in booms
72.x: Counter-cyclical – Deficits in slumps (Atma Nirbhar Bharat, 2020), consolidation in booms

72.s: What is a recession followed by a short-lived recovery and another recession called?
72.x: Double-dip recession – Recession → short-lived recovery → another recession; an ordinary recession = two consecutive quarters of falling GDP

72.s: To what was CENVAT cut in the December 2008 stimulus package?
72.x: December 2008 stimulus package – CENVAT cut by 4 percentage points, 14% → 10% (to 8% in February 2009) to soften the global slowdown

72.s: What is it called when government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment?
72.x: Crowding out – Government borrowing raises interest rates, reducing private investment

72.s: What is it called when public capex draws in private investment?
72.x: Crowding in – Public capex draws private investment

72.s: What is the change in GDP divided by the change in government spending or taxes called?
72.x: Fiscal multiplier – Change in GDP ÷ change in govt spending or taxes

72.s: What is the capex multiplier in India, the largest among spending types?
72.x: Capex multiplier – 2.5-3 in India – largest for capital expenditure

72.s: Which ratio shows the quality of the deficit?
72.x: Quality of deficit – High RD/FD ratio = borrowing funds consumption; 2026-27 RD 1.5 / FD 4.3 ≈ one-third

72.s: Which of these is a spending-side measure to reduce the deficit?
72.x: Spending – Downsizing bureaucracy, reducing revenue expenditure, rationalising subsidies through DBT, cutting unproductive spending

72.s: Which of these is a receipts-side measure to reduce the deficit?
72.x: Receipts – Selling/offloading PSU shares (disinvestment), widening the tax base

72.s: Which of these adds to the fiscal deficit?
72.x: FDI inflows and privatising higher education do not cut the deficit; new welfare schemes add to it.

72.s: How large are subsidies in Indian agriculture compared with developed countries?
72.x: Financial subsidy – A big source of budget deficit; subsidies in Indian agriculture are lower than in developed countries

72.s: What share of Union expenditure goes to subsidies in 2026-27?
72.x: Major heads – Food, fertiliser, petroleum (LPG); total subsidies ≈ 8.5% of Union expenditure (2026-27)

72.s: Which is the largest fertiliser subsidy item?
72.x: Urea – Largest fertiliser subsidy item

72.s: Which machines record fertiliser sales for subsidy payment under fertiliser DBT (2018)?
72.x: Fertiliser DBT (2018) – Paid to companies after retail sale on PoS machines with Aadhaar authentication

72.s: Which of these is a hidden subsidy?
72.x: Hidden subsidies – Tax concessions, cheap credit, under-priced health and education (forex reserves are not a subsidy head)

72.s: How much did major subsidies rise in Q1 FY27 on crude prices?
72.x: Q1 FY27 – Major subsidies up 37.4% on crude prices

72.s: What kind of approach does development need, per the notes?
72.x: Development needs a multi-dimensional approach; the Government focuses on both micro and macro issues.

72.s: Which is the main source of financing the fiscal deficit?
72.x: Sources – Market borrowings (G-Secs), T-bills, small savings/NSSF, State Provident Funds, external debt, draw-down of cash

72.s: What share of the fiscal deficit do domestic borrowings finance?
72.x: Domestic borrowings – Fill most of the FD (about 98-99%); 2026-27 BE: net market borrowings ₹11.73 lakh crore of ₹16.96 lakh crore; external debt only ₹15,385 crore

72.s: What replaced ad hoc T-bills from 1 April 1997?
72.x: Ad hoc T-bills – Automatic monetisation from the mid-1950s; 1994 RBI-Government agreement; abolished 31 March 1997; WMA from 1 April 1997

72.s: What is a Ways and Means Advance beyond the limit called?
72.x: Ways and Means Advances (WMA) – Temporary RBI advances to cover short gaps between receipts and payments; WMA beyond the limit = overdraft

72.s: From which year has the RBI been barred from subscribing to primary issues of G-Secs?
72.x: RBI in primary issues – Barred from 2006-07 from subscribing to primary issues of G-Secs, except under the escape clause

72.s: What was the largest source of the 8th Plan's public outlay?
72.x: 8th Plan – Public outlay ₹4,34,100 crore – largest source government borrowings (46.6%)

72.s: Why are PSU dividends not a source of financing the fiscal deficit?
72.x: PSU dividends – Non-tax revenue, not a source of financing the fiscal deficit

72.s: At which exchange rates does the debt statement value external debt since the 2018 FRBM definition?
72.x: External liabilities in the Union Budget are shown at historical (book-value) exchange rates; since the 2018 FRBM debt definition the debt statement also values external debt at current exchange rates.

72.s: What does a rising fiscal deficit-to-GDP ratio do to private investment?
72.x: Continued high borrowing kept real interest rates high; rising FD/GDP crowds out private investment; interest payments = single largest item of non-plan revenue expenditure.

72.s: What is the twin deficit?
72.x: Best way to finance a current account deficit = FDI; twin deficit = FD + CAD (dissaving cuts national savings).

72.s: What is a budget where revenue equals expenditure called?
72.x: Balanced – Revenue = expenditure

72.s: What is a budget in which receipts exceed expenditure called?
72.x: Surplus – Receipts > expenditure

72.s: What is a budget in which expenditure exceeds receipts called?
72.x: Deficit – Expenditure > receipts

72.s: Who developed zero-based budgeting?
72.x: Zero-based – Every scheme reviewed and justified afresh, no base from last year; Peter Pyhrr, Jimmy Carter; introduced in India

72.s: Which budget links spending to work done through unit costs and performance standards?
72.x: Performance – Spending linked to work done – work management, unit costs, performance standards (not personnel selection)

72.s: In which year did India present its first outcome budget?
72.x: Outcome – Outlays against measurable results; first 2005-06

72.s: With which Union Budget was the first Gender Budget Statement presented?
72.x: Gender – First Gender Budget Statement with Union Budget 2005-06

72.s: Which of these is non-tax revenue?
72.x: Revenue – Tax and non-tax (e.g. PSU dividends)

72.s: Which of these is a non-debt capital receipt?
72.x: Capital – non-debt – Recovery of loans, disinvestment, asset monetisation

72.s: Which of these is a debt capital receipt?
72.x: Capital – debt – Market borrowings, small savings, other liabilities

72.s: How many paise of every rupee received come from borrowings and other liabilities in Budget 2026-27?
72.x: Budget 2026-27 – Borrowings and other liabilities = 24 paise of every rupee received – largest single item

72.s: Which of these is non-developmental expenditure?
72.x: Developmental vs non-developmental – Non-developmental = interest, defence, administration

72.s: Which of these is charged expenditure, not voted by Parliament?
72.x: Charged (Art. 112(3)) – Not voted by Parliament: President's emoluments, debt charges, SC judges' salaries

73.s: How is deficit financing done in the Indian sense?
73.x: Indian – Budget gap met by borrowing from the RBI; RBI creates new money – the government "buys money" from the RBI

73.s: How is a budget deficit mainly financed in the Western sense?
o: Borrowing from the public and market
73.x: Western – Any financing of a budget deficit, mainly borrowing from the public/market

73.s: What is the main effect of deficit financing on money?
73.x: Effect – Increase in money supply; creates extra paper currency

73.s: What does deficit financing finance?
73.x: Deficit financing – Financing a deficit budget – spending in excess of revenue (total expenditure > total receipts) and sustaining that gap

73.s: What must be added to the budgetary deficit to get the fiscal deficit?
o: Net increase in internal and external borrowings and other liabilities
73.x: Fiscal deficit (Union Budget) – Budgetary deficit + net increase in internal and external borrowings and other liabilities

73.s: What is an economic unit that spends more than it receives in a period called?
73.x: Deficit unit – An economic unit that spends more than it receives in a period

73.s: What did deficit financing finance as a "pragmatic tool" in India?
73.x: Purpose – Raising resources for economic development – a "pragmatic tool" to finance the Five Year Plans (not redemption of public debt, BoP adjustment or cutting foreign debt)

73.s: When need deficit financing not be inflationary?
o: In small doses for productive investment
73.x: Inflation – Small doses for productive investment need not be inflationary; an often-used tool for financing budget deficits

73.s: Which of these made deficit financing necessary after 1947?
73.x: Why needed after 1947 – Low tax base, poor compliance, weak private banking and low domestic savings

73.s: For what was deficit financing used as a remedy in Indian planning?
73.x: Objectives – Remedy for depression, raise aggregate demand, subsidies, anti-poverty programmes, PSU losses

73.s: How did deficit financing rank as a source of public-sector Plan outlay in the Eighth Plan?
73.x: Eighth Plan – Largest source of financing public-sector Plan outlay – ahead of external borrowing

73.s: How much was deficit financing used from Independence to the late 1960s?
73.x: Independence to late 1960s – Little use, to fund plans

73.s: About how much deficit financing was used in the Second Plan?
73.x: Second Plan – About ₹1,100 crore against ₹1,200 crore planned

73.s: What did the Third Plan say about reliance on deficit financing?
o: It was to be strictly limited
73.x: Third Plan – Reliance to be strictly limited

73.s: What did heavy reliance on deficit financing from the 1970s lead to?
73.x: 1970s onwards – Heavy reliance (oil shocks, welfare spending) led to debt and inflation

73.s: Which of these is a method of deficit financing?
o: Running down cash balances with the RBI
73.x: Running down cash balances with the RBI; issue of new currency; borrowing from the RBI (RBI prints notes); also internal and external borrowing, external aid and grants.

73.s: Which source comes last in the order of preference for financing a deficit?
73.x: Order of preference: external aid/grants → external borrowing → internal borrowing → printing currency (last resort, most inflationary).

73.s: What is borrowing from the RBI through fresh currency called?
73.x: Monetised deficit: borrowing from the RBI through fresh currency (high-powered money); the FRBM Act disallows it in normal times.

73.s: Which method of financing a deficit is the most inflationary?
73.x: Creation of new money – Most inflationary

73.s: How inflationary is deficit financing by borrowing from banks?
73.x: Borrowing from banks – High

73.s: Why is borrowing from the public less inflationary?
73.x: Borrowing from public – Lower – uses existing savings

73.s: What is the effect of repaying public debt on prices?
73.x: Repayment of public debt – Not inflationary – withdraws money

73.s: What does deficit financing do to the money supply?
73.x: Deficit financing is inflationary in character; it increases the money supply; if it fails to raise output it generates inflation.

73.s: What began automatic RBI financing of the government in the mid-1950s?
73.x: Mid-1950s – Ad hoc Treasury Bills – automatic RBI financing of the government begins

73.s: What cap on ad hoc T-bills was agreed for 1994-95?
73.x: Sep 1994 – RBI-Government agreement begins phasing out ad hoc T-bills (₹6,000 crore cap for 1994-95)

73.s: When were ad hoc T-bills abolished?
73.x: 31 Mar 1997 – Ad hoc T-bills abolished; Ways and Means Advances (WMA) from 1 April 1997

73.s: Which Act came in 2003 to control deficit financing?
73.x: 2003 – FRBM Act

73.s: In which year: RBI barred from subscribing to primary issues of G-Secs?
73.x: 1 Apr 2006 – RBI barred from subscribing to primary issues of G-Secs

73.s: What is the escape-clause deviation cap on the fiscal deficit under the 2018 FRBM amendment?
73.x: 2018 – Monetised borrowing only on escape-clause grounds; deviation cap 0.5% of GDP a year

73.s: What does a sale of G-Secs by the RBI do to liquidity?
73.x: Market borrowing replaces it; liquidity is managed by OMOs: sale of G-Secs drains liquidity, purchase adds it. 15 Sep 2026: RBI announced OMO sales of ₹1 lakh crore with 91/182/364-day T-bill auctions.

73.s: On which date did the RBI announce OMO sales of ₹1 lakh crore with 91/182/364-day T-bill auctions?
73.x: Market borrowing replaces it; liquidity is managed by OMOs: sale of G-Secs drains liquidity, purchase adds it. 15 Sep 2026: RBI announced OMO sales of ₹1 lakh crore with 91/182/364-day T-bill auctions.

73.s: Which method of financing a deficit comes last in the order of preference, being the most inflationary?
73.x: Order of preference: external aid/grants → external borrowing → internal borrowing → printing currency (last resort, most inflationary).

73.s: What is the fresh currency created when the government borrows from the RBI (monetised deficit) called?
73.x: Monetised deficit – Borrowing from the RBI through fresh currency (high-powered money); the FRBM Act disallows it in normal times

73.s: Why is deficit financing inflationary in character?
73.x: Deficit financing is inflationary in character: it increases the money supply, and if it fails to raise output it generates inflation.

73.s: What does the sale of G-Secs by the RBI through open market operations do to liquidity?
73.x: Market borrowing and liquidity – Managed by OMOs: sale of G-Secs drains liquidity, purchase adds it

73.s: Which kind of inflation arises when money supply and demand rise without more goods and services?
73.x: Demand-pull inflation – Money supply and demand rise without more goods and services; hurts the poor most

73.s: What is the effect called when heavy government market borrowing raises interest rates and cuts private investment?
73.x: Crowding out – Market borrowing raises interest rates, cuts private investment

73.s: What is the situation called when a government borrows just to make interest payments, leaving little room for health and education?
73.x: Debt trap – Government borrows to make interest payments; little room for health, education

73.s: Which is a consequence of excessive deficit financing?
73.x: Others – Adverse effect on savings and investment, rising inequality, BoP deficit, higher cost of production

73.s: What follows a sovereign rating downgrade caused by high deficits?
o: Higher borrowing cost for government and firms
73.x: Rating downgrades – Higher borrowing cost for government and firms

73.s: Under which head of public debt do market loans, Treasury Bills and special securities to NSSF fall?
73.x: Internal debt – Market loans, Treasury Bills, special securities to NSSF

73.s: Which head: Small savings, State Provident Funds, reserve funds and deposits?
73.x: Other liabilities (Public Account) – Small savings, State Provident Funds, reserve funds and deposits

73.s: Under which head of public debt are loans from foreign sources counted?
73.x: External debt – Loans from foreign sources

73.s: How much of every rupee spent by the Centre goes to interest payments in Budget 2026-27?
73.x: Interest (Budget 2026-27) – 20 paise of every rupee spent; about 40% of revenue receipts

73.s: How much had States borrowed till October 2025 (62% of their FY26 plan)?
73.x: State borrowing – ₹5.23 trillion till Oct 2025 (62% of FY26 plan); RBI wants a shift from subsidies to capital expenditure

73.s: What was Andhra Pradesh's fiscal deficit in 2024-25 as a share of GSDP, against the 4% limit?
73.x: AP – Fiscal deficit 2024-25 5.05% of GSDP vs 4% limit; market loans ≈ 75% of AP's debt – after bifurcation AP met its heavy deficit mainly through market loans

74.s: What does the abbreviation FRBM in the FRBM Act stand for?
74.x: Name – Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act

74.s: Who was the Finance Minister when the FRBM Bill was introduced in 2000?
74.x: Bill – Introduced 2000 (Vajpayee Government; FM Yashwant Sinha)

74.s: On which date was the FRBM Act enacted?
74.x: Enacted / in force – 26 August 2003; in force (with Rules) 5 July 2004

74.s: Which two deficits does the FRBM Act aim to reduce?
74.x: Aim – Fiscal discipline and prudence by reducing revenue and fiscal deficits and public debt – it concerns both FD and RD

74.s: Which objective of the FRBM Act concerns fairness between present and future generations?
74.x: Objectives – Inter-generational equity, long-run macro stability, eliminate RD, cut FD, debt management, transparency (fixing the repo rate is not one)

74.s: What type of reform is the FRBM Act, as distinct from post-1991 financial-sector reforms like SARFAESI?
74.x: Type of reform – Fiscal – not one of the post-1991 financial-sector reforms (capital adequacy, NPA norms, SARFAESI)

74.s: Who presented the first Budget of India in 1860?
74.x: First Budget of India – James Wilson, 1860

74.s: What fiscal deficit target (as a share of GDP) did the original FRBM Act set?
74.x: Fiscal deficit – 3% of GDP – by 31 March 2008 in the Act, later 31 March 2009

74.s: What was the original FRBM target for the revenue deficit by 31 March 2008 (later 2009)?
74.x: Revenue deficit – Eliminated – 31 March 2008, revised to 31 March 2009

74.s: What yearly cut in the fiscal deficit did the FRBM Rules 2004 require?
74.x: Annual cut (Rules 2004) – FD 0.3%, RD 0.5% of GDP a year

74.s: What yearly cap did the original FRBM targets put on extra guarantees on the Consolidated Fund?
74.x: Guarantees – Extra guarantees on Consolidated Fund ≤ 0.5% of GDP a year

74.s: From which year was the RBI barred from subscribing to primary issues of central G-Secs under the FRBM Act?
74.x: RBI – Centre not to borrow from RBI except WMA; RBI out of primary G-Sec issues from 2006-07

74.s: Which of these was never a target under the FRBM Act?
74.x: Elimination of primary deficit – Never an FRBM target

74.s: Where did the public-debt cap of 50% of GDP by 2011 appear?
74.x: Public-debt cap of 50% of GDP by 2011 – In the FRBM Bill, 2000, not in the Act as passed

74.s: How many fiscal indicators does the Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement under FRBM track?
74.x: Tax-GDP – Not a legal target; one of the four indicators in the MTFP Statement (RD, FD, tax-GDP, total outstanding liabilities)

74.s: When did the FRBM Act (as revised) require the Centre to cut the fiscal deficit to 3% and phase out the revenue deficit?
74.x: Under the Act the Centre had to cut FD to 3% and phase out RD by March 2009, keep transparency and limit RBI borrowing; States' failures are not part of its targets.

74.s: Which law mandates the Macro-Economic Framework Statement presented with the Union Budget?
74.x: Macro-Economic Framework – Growth, inflation, fiscal and external balance, assumptions – mandated by the FRBM Act (not by Art. 112/113 or convention)

74.s: What kind of period does the Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement use for its targets on RD, FD and tax-GDP?
74.x: Medium-Term Fiscal Policy – 3-year rolling targets for RD, FD, tax-GDP, total outstanding liabilities

74.s: Which FRBM statement under Section 3 sets out the tax, spending and borrowing strategy?
74.x: Fiscal Policy Strategy – Tax, spending, borrowing strategy

74.s: In which year was the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework Statement added under the FRBM Act?
74.x: Medium-Term Expenditure Framework – 3-year expenditure ceilings; added 2012, laid after the Budget

74.s: Under which provision is the Annual Financial Statement laid before Parliament?
74.x: Annual Financial Statement – Laid under Art. 112, not under the FRBM Act

74.s: Since when have the FRBM rolling targets been suspended?
74.x: Rolling targets – Suspended since 2021-22; Budget 2026-27 laid the MEFS and a combined MTFPS-cum-FPSS

74.s: What did the FRBM Act make a legal duty of the government?
74.x: Significance – Made fiscal discipline a legal duty and added disclosure statements to the Budget

74.s: In which Budget was the FRBM review committee (N.K. Singh) announced?
74.x: Timeline – Announced Budget 2016-17; formed May 2016; report January 2017; reflected in Budget 2017-18

74.s: Who chaired the FRBM review committee announced in Budget 2016-17?
74.x: Members – Five: chair N.K. Singh; Sumit Bose, Urjit Patel, Rathin Roy among them

74.s: Which indicator did the N.K. Singh committee make the principal anchor of fiscal policy?
74.x: Principal anchor – Debt-to-GDP; FD = operational target

74.s: What general government debt target by 2023 did the N.K. Singh committee recommend?
74.x: General govt debt – 60% by 2023 = Centre 40% + States 20%

74.s: When did the N.K. Singh committee want the 3% fiscal deficit phase (of three years) to end?
74.x: FD – 3% for the next three years (to 2019-20/March 2020), then 2.5% by 2022-23

74.s: What revenue deficit target by 2023 did the N.K. Singh committee recommend?
What institution did the N.K. Singh committee recommend for fiscal oversight?
o: A Debt Management Office under RBI
74.x: Institution – Independent, advisory Fiscal Council (no binding powers)

74.s: How much deviation from the fiscal deficit target did the N.K. Singh committee allow under its escape clause?
74.x: Escape clause – Deviation up to 0.5% of GDP; trigger includes far-reaching structural reforms

74.s: When did the 2018 FRBM amendment require Central government debt to fall to 40% of GDP?
74.x: Debt anchor – General govt 60%, Centre 40% by 31 March 2025; FD 3% by 31 March 2021

74.s: Which target did the 2018 FRBM amendment drop?
74.x: Targets – Debt and fiscal deficit together; revenue deficit (and ERD) target dropped

74.s: What fall in real growth below the previous four quarters' average triggers the FRBM escape clause?
74.x: Escape grounds – National security, war, national calamity, agricultural collapse, structural reforms, sharp output fall – real growth 3 percentage points below the average of the previous four quarters; not a routine tax shortfall

74.s: What is the maximum yearly fiscal deviation allowed under the escape clause of the 2018 FRBM amendment?
